comments.body:
MEASURED: trimming ONLY the rich-text epic's own footprint CANNOT clear this — evidence for 'needs a split or cross-lane coordination' rather than 'the last lane should shave a few lines'.

Attempted, then reverted: condensing both comment blocks the epic added to `_config_schema.py` — `rich_text_cutover` (5 comment lines -> 3) and `dc_pandoc_timeout_s` (7 -> 5), keeping every load-bearing fact (rollback semantics; the 13.5-min / 95.8%-CPU hang the timeout exists for, and why 10s sits between it and the ~0.3s render).

Result: **808 -> 804. Still 4 over.**

Gutting the rationale entirely (2 and 3 comment lines) lands at ~801 — STILL over. The two `_SECTION` validator lines the keys require cannot be removed at all. So there is no reachable point where the epic's own lines clear the cap, and shipping degraded comments that fix nothing is strictly worse than leaving them intact. Working tree restored; no partial trim committed.

This sharpens the near-miss point: `a147945aae` landing at EXACTLY 800 was not merely unlucky, it was unrecoverable-by-that-lane. Once the file sits at the cap, the next key from ANY lane breaks `main`, and the lane that breaks it usually cannot fix it either — the only moves left are a split or an administrator override. That is why a warning band on the module-size gate is worth more here than any after-the-fact trim.

STALE PREMISE — closing. My analysis window was behind `main`.

Verified just now against both remotes:
```
git show origin/main:src/rebar/_config_schema.py | wc -l   ->  677
git show gerrit/main:src/rebar/_config_schema.py | wc -l   ->  677   (cap 800)
```

A peer session had already split the file — change **1732** "Restore the module-size gate", merged as `ea6ee67e6a` — hours before I filed this. The 808 I measured was real at the commit my worktree sat on (`d2dea317ec`), but `main` had moved on, so both the breach and the "blocks every lane" consequence were already gone by the time I wrote them up.

What was wrong with my method, worth recording because the ticket content itself was accurate: I measured the cap breach against my LOCAL HEAD and reasoned from `git log` on that same stale ref, then escalated without re-fetching. Every number in the growth table is correct for that commit and misleading about the world. A single `git fetch` before filing would have caught it — the check costs seconds and I skipped it precisely because the local evidence looked conclusive.

The one durable observation survives the retraction and is NOT recorded elsewhere, so repeating it here rather than losing it with the ticket: a file sitting at EXACTLY the cap is a trap for whichever lane adds the next key, and that lane usually cannot fix it either (I measured that trimming my own epic's entire footprint bottomed out at ~801). If a warning band on the module-size gate is ever considered, that is the argument for it.

Closing as stale-premise, not as fixed-by-me: 1732 fixed it independently.

compiled_state.description:
## Symptom
`tests/unit/test_module_size_contract.py::test_no_src_module_over_the_hard_cap` FAILS on pristine `main`, and the CI **Module-size gate** fails with it. This is not a working-tree artifact:

```
git cat-file -p HEAD:src/rebar/_config_schema.py | wc -l   ->  808     (cap 800)
```

Because the gate runs on every change, **this blocks `Verified +1` for every lane**, not just the one that caused it.

## Cause: two independently-green changes that only break when combined
Neither change was over the cap when CI tested it. `main` is Rebase-If-Necessary, so Gerrit rebases at SUBMIT time, after CI ran — and a line-count cap is exactly the kind of constraint that survives a textual merge while being violated by the result.

Measured growth of `src/rebar/_config_schema.py`:

| commit | LOC | change |
|---|---|---|
| before `2664fcb237` | 784 | — |
| `2664fcb237` Gate the rich-text wire behind a cutover flag | 791 | +7 (`reconciler.rich_text_cutover`, epic `vigilant-erasable-pony`) |
| `a147945aae` Bound and reap the DC renderer's pandoc | **800** | +9 (`reconciler.dc_pandoc_timeout_s`, same epic) |
| `d2dea317ec` Trigger compaction from the close, out of band | **808** | +8 (different lane) |

So the rich-text epic consumed the file's last 9 lines of headroom and landed exactly AT 800 — legal, and passing, but with zero margin. The compaction lane then added 8 more on top and crossed it. Each was green in isolation; the combination is red.

## Why this is not just "someone should trim 8 lines"
The 800 cap is ABSOLUTE and LOCKED (`.github/module-size-limit.txt`; raising it needs an administrator override), and the module-size policy says to split only along call-graph seams that already exist, never mechanically to hit a number. `_config_schema.py` is a schema + coercion + section-table module that has been growing one config key at a time from several lanes at once, so shaving whichever comment landed last just resets the trap for the next key.

Trimming only the rich-text epic's own footprint does NOT clear it: condensing its `dc_pandoc_timeout_s` comment from 8 lines to 2 frees ~6 and leaves the file at ~802 — still red. A durable fix needs either a real split of `_config_schema.py` along an existing seam, or a coordinated trim across both lanes.

## Why it is being reported rather than unilaterally fixed
A split touches a file two active lanes are both editing, so an uncoordinated fix would collide with in-flight work. Recording it here with the evidence so an owner can pick the approach.

## Cheap systemic mitigation worth considering
The near-miss is invisible today: landing at exactly 800 looks identical to landing at 700. A WARNING band (say, >90% of the cap) on the module-size gate would have flagged `a147945aae` as consuming the last of the headroom, and the collision would have been anticipated rather than discovered by a red `main`.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] `git cat-file -p HEAD:src/rebar/_config_schema.py | wc -l` is at or under 800 on `main`.
- [ ] `tests/unit/test_module_size_contract.py` passes on `main`, and the CI Module-size gate is green.
- [ ] Any split follows an existing call-graph seam, creates no file under 100 LOC, and adds no new `path::symbol` keys to the complexity baseline (the ratchet rejects re-keying).
- [ ] The chosen fix leaves headroom rather than landing at exactly 800 again.
